newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Laws to curb Asia FX market would hit investment.
newsitem.headline: Laws to curb Asia FX market would hit investment.

text.p: Malaysian prime minister Mahathir Mohamad's verbal attack on currency speculators on Thursday contained a threat to enact laws to curb speculative attacks on Asian regional currencies.
But it is hard to see quite what could be done legally apart from draconian capital controls, which would be massively counterproductive in terms of investment in the region, analysts said.
"If you look at what they could do technically it would be severe," said Kobus Van Der Wath, regional head of treasury economics at Standard Chartered in Singapore.

Anything on the lines of regional currency controls would send a strong signal to investors to be very careful and they would start to wonder about repatriation of profits and dividends and worry about what happens when they liquidated holdings.

"Talking about controls without any easy controls to hand points to a plunge into foreign exchange controls and that would change the whole investment profile for the entire region in the blink of an eye," Van Der Wath added.

Thursday's action on the Asian foreign exchanges would seem to back up this argument with traders and analysts noting that much of the immediate pressure on currencies was due to portfolio hedging and not short selling by speculators.

The Thai baht, Singapore dollar and Malaysian dollar all fell sharply as already nervous fund managers decided to hedge a greater portion of their portfolios, with the Hong Kong dollar also hit by forward selling.
"What's happening now is genuine portfolio hedging and genuine concern as opposed to having a speculative play," said Tim Lucas, treasury manager at Bank of Bermuda in Hong Kong.

Southeast Asian countries, particularly those running a current account deficit, rely on an inward capital flow and without investor confidence that cash could be moved quickly and easily this flow would be turned off.
Slapping on capital controls may deter speculators but it would also deter investment, analsyts said.

Aside from legal moves like capital controls, the Southeast Asian countries could get an umbrella body like the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to take a more central role in coordinating central banks to achieve individual objectives.
Other alternatives include firmer agreements of mutual help during times of crisis or maybe a pool of liquid assets which could be mobilised to defend currencies.
Even if the market has got hold of the wrong end of the stick with regard to Mahathir's hard line comments, acute nervousness in the market has meant they have been interpreted negatively.

"There is a fear in the market that more drastic measures could be put in place by the Asian central banks and at worse this could take the form of capital controls," said Andy Tan, economist at MMS International in Singapore.
"Which would be quite negative in terms of the openness of the economies around the region."
